items.title: Test free chlorine today
items.because: ORP is 453 mV, well under the 550 mV mark where the water may genuinely not be sanitising. Free chlorine isn't measured -- the ICO can't read it -- so nobody knows whether that is a real chlorine shortage or just the proxy sagging. pH and Salt are out of band, which depresses ORP on its own, so this may resolve once they are fixed. It is still worth a strip test today rather than assuming.
items.why: ORP at 453 mV is low enough that the water might not be sanitizing, but you don't actually have a free chlorine number today since the ICO can't read it. pH sitting at 8 and salt at 2,616 ppm can both drag ORP down on their own, so a strip test tells you whether you actually have a chlorine shortage before you add anything to fix one.
items.how: Dip a free-chlorine test strip in water at elbow depth, away from the return jets, and read it against the bottle's color chart in the time it specifies. Do this before deciding whether you need the holding dose of chlorine later on the list.

items.title: Add salt
items.because: Salt is 2,616 ppm, below the 2800-3200 ppm the cell needs. A cell run under its salt band makes less chlorine and wears out faster.
items.why: Salt is at 2,616 ppm, under the 2,800-3,200 ppm band the cell needs to work properly. Below that band the cell makes less chlorine per hour and wears itself down doing it, so the shortfall compounds the longer salt stays low.
items.how: Predissolve the salt in a 5-gallon bucket of pool water first — granules left sitting on the vinyl floor will bleach and weaken it. With the pump running, broadcast the dissolved slurry slowly around the deep end, well clear of the skimmer, and let it circulate.

dose.label: 57.5 lb of salt (about 1.44 of a 40 lb bag)

items.title: Bring pH down
items.because: pH is 8, above the 7.6-7.8 target. TA wasn't measured, so this dose assumes a mid-band buffer -- treat it as a starting point and retest.
items.why: pH is at 8, above the 7.6-7.8 target, and high pH wastes the chlorine the cell makes — part of why ORP is only 453 mV today. TA wasn't measured, so this dose assumes a mid-band buffer; treat today's number as a starting point and retest once it's circulated.
items.how: Wear gloves and eye protection, and add the acid to a bucket of water first — never water into the acid. With the pump running, pour the diluted acid slowly around the deep end, never into the skimmer, since neat acid run through the skimmer eats the pump, heater, and salt cell.

dose.label: 31 fl oz (3.88 cups) of muriatic acid

items.title: Backwash the filter
items.because: Never logged. The target cadence is every 14 days -- log it once and the clock starts.
items.why: You've never logged a backwash, so there's no clock running on it. The target cadence is every 14 days — logging today gives you a starting point to track from.
items.how: Shut the pump off, turn the multiport valve to backwash, then restart the pump and run it until the sight glass runs clear. Switch to rinse for about 30 seconds to reseat the sand bed, then turn the valve back to filter and resume normal operation.

items.title: If you can't test, add a holding dose
items.because: If you can't test today, 0.25 gal of 12.5% liquid chlorine raises free chlorine by about 1.5 ppm. That is a holding dose, not a shock: 2 ppm is below what you would swim in, so it cannot over-chlorinate the pool, and it buys a day without pretending to know what the level actually is. Test before adding any more than this. Acid is on today's list too: wait at least 4 hours after the acid before this goes in, and never put them in together.
items.why: This only matters if you skip today's strip test: 0.25 gallon of 12.5% liquid chlorine lifts free chlorine by about 1.5 ppm, a holding dose meant to bridge one day, not a shock — it can't push the pool past what's safe to swim in. Treat it as a stopgap and test before adding any more.
items.how: Wait at least four hours after you pour the acid before this goes in — acid and chlorine move pH in opposite directions, and doing them close together muddies what the water actually did. When you do add it, keep the pump running and pour it slowly around the deep end, away from the skimmer, and never combine it with the acid in the same bucket since that produces chlorine gas.

items.title: Leave the cell alone for now
items.because: ORP is 453 mV, under the at least 600 mV floor -- but pH and Salt are out of band too, and ORP sits downstream of all of it. Fix those first, give the water a full day to circulate, then re-read. Turning the cell up now just means running it harder against the same problem.
items.why: ORP at 453 mV is under the 600 mV floor, but pH and salt are both out of band right now and ORP sits downstream of both — pushing the cell harder today just runs it against the same two problems. Give today's salt and acid doses a full day to circulate, then reread before touching the cell.
items.how: Leave the cell's output dial where it is today rather than reaching for it. Let the pump keep running so the salt and acid mix through the water, and check again with tomorrow's reading.

items.title: The cell is already flat out
items.because: The cell is at 100% (from config.json), running 24 hours a day, so there is no headroom left to ask for -- this is not a setting you can turn up. pH and Salt are out of band, and each of those starves the cell in its own way: low salt gives it less to work with, high pH wastes the chlorine it makes, low CYA lets the sun burn it off. Fix those and the same cell will produce more.
items.why: The cell is already running flat out — 100% output, 24 hours a day — so there's no setting left to turn up even if ORP is still low. Low salt and high pH are both starving that same cell of what it needs to make chlorine efficiently; fix those and the existing setting will produce more on its own.
items.how: There's no dial move to make here today. Focus on the salt and acid doses instead, and let the cell run as it already is while the water catches up.

items.title: Leave the pump schedule alone for now
items.because: The pump is running 24 hours a day, which is a lot -- but on a saltwater pool the pump schedule is the chlorine schedule, because the cell only makes chlorine while water is going through it. With ORP at 453 mV, cutting hours would cut production exactly when you need it. Get ORP comfortably over 600 with the cell below full, and that is the moment to start trimming hours and watching what happens.
items.why: The pump is already running 24 hours a day, and since the cell only makes chlorine while water passes through it, the pump schedule is effectively the chlorine schedule on this pool. Cutting hours now, with ORP at 453 mV, would cut production right when it's needed most.
items.how: Leave the pump timer at 24 hours for now. Once ORP is comfortably over 600 mV with the cell running below full output, that's the day to start trimming an hour at a time and watching what happens.

items.title: Test borates
items.because: Borates aren't on the ICO panel and haven't been tested. The target is 50 ppm; a strip test once a season is enough to know where you are.
items.why: Borates aren't on the ICO panel and have never been tested, so you don't actually know where you stand against the 50 ppm target. It only needs checking about once a season, so today's a fine day to get a baseline.
items.how: Dip a borate test strip in water away from the return jets and compare it to the bottle's color chart. Log whatever it reads so you have a number to work from next time.

safety_rules: NEVER pour undiluted acid into the skimmer. Acid down the skimmer runs neat through the pump, heater and salt cell and eats them. Dilute it and pour it slowly around the deep end with the pump running.

NEVER put shock and acid in the same session without at least 4 hours between them, and say the gap out loud in the instructions. Both move pH hard in opposite directions, and back to back you cannot tell what the water actually did.
ALWAYS predissolve dry chemicals in a 5-gallon bucket of pool water before they go in. Undissolved granules sitting on a vinyl liner bleach and weaken it.
NEVER put chlorine and acid in the same bucket, in either order. That combination produces chlorine gas.
ALWAYS add acid to water, never water to acid -- pouring water into acid can boil and spit it back at you.
The pump must be RUNNING before anything goes in, and keep running afterwards, so a dose disperses instead of sitting in one corner.
headline: Salt and pH need fixing before ORP can recover
summary: This morning's reading is fresh, so every dose below is computed off current water. pH is high at 8 and salt is low at 2,616 ppm, both dragging ORP down to 453 mV — fix those two today, test free chlorine so you're not guessing, and leave the cell and pump schedule alone until tomorrow's reading shows whether it worked.
